question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to the famous Section 125 CrPC for order of maintenance?
options: Section 144 BNSS
Section 125 BNSS
Section 163 BNSS
Section 187 BNSS
explanation: Section 144 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 125 CrPC (order for maintenance of wives, children and parents).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 144 BNSS corresponds to Section 125 CrPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Section 125 BNSS is security for keeping peace upon conviction.

learningObjective: Map Section 125 CrPC to Section 144 BNSS.

question: Under Section 144(1) BNSS (Section 125(1) CrPC), who can claim maintenance?
options: Wife unable to maintain herself; legitimate/illegitimate minor child; child with physical/mental abnormality; father or mother unable to maintain himself/herself
Only a legally wedded wife living with the husband
Only minors below 12 years
Any unemployed relative
explanation: Section 144(1) BNSS / S. 125(1) CrPC specifies four categories: (a) wife; (b) minor child; (c) major abnormal child; (d) father or mother unable to maintain themselves.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; wife, minor child, major disabled child, father or mother.
optionBreakdown.B: Divorced wife not remarried also included; living together not mandatory if separate for just ground.

learningObjective: Recall eligible claimants for maintenance.

question: How is 'Wife' defined in Explanation (b) to Section 144(1) BNSS (Section 125(1) CrPC)?
options: Includes a woman who has been divorced by, or has obtained a divorce from, her husband and has not remarried
Only a woman whose marriage is actively subsisting
Includes a live-in partner who never married
Includes a woman who has remarried another man
explanation: Explanation (b) to S. 144(1) BNSS / S. 125(1) CrPC expressly clarifies that 'wife' includes a divorced woman who has not remarried.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; divorced wife who has not remarried is included.
optionBreakdown.C: Live-in partner covered under DV Act, not strictly S. 125.
optionBreakdown.D: Remarried wife cannot claim under S. 125.

provision: BNSS S. 144(1) Expl (b) / CrPC S. 125(1) Expl (b)
learningObjective: Understand statutory definition of wife including divorced wife.

question: Under Section 144(4) BNSS (Section 125(4) CrPC), in which of the following circumstances is a wife NOT entitled to receive maintenance?
options: If she is living in adultery, or if without any sufficient reason she refuses to live with her husband, or if they are living separately by mutual consent
If she has passed higher education
If her parents are wealthy
If she filed an FIR under Section 498A IPC
explanation: Section 144(4) BNSS / S. 125(4) CrPC bars maintenance if wife: (1) is living in adultery; (2) refuses without sufficient reason; or (3) lives separately by mutual consent.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; three statutory disqualifications under subsection (4).
optionBreakdown.D: Filing matrimonial complaint is not a bar.

learningObjective: Master statutory disqualifications to maintenance.

question: In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum ((1985) 2 SCC 556), what did the Constitution Bench hold regarding Section 125 CrPC?
options: Section 125 CrPC is a secular provision of social justice that applies to all citizens irrespective of religion, and a Muslim husband is liable to maintain his divorced wife unable to maintain herself
Section 125 does not apply to Muslims
Maintenance ceases strictly upon expiry of iddat period in all cases
Muslim wives can only approach the Waqf Board
explanation: Shah Bano established that Section 125 is a secular, overarching social welfare statute taking precedence over personal laws.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Shah Bano established secular universality of Section 125.

learningObjective: Master Shah Bano secular maintenance ruling.

question: In Danial Latifi v. Union of India ((2001) 7 SCC 740), how did the Supreme Court interpret the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986?
options: Upheld the Act by holding that the husband must make reasonable and fair provision within the iddat period for the entire future life of the divorced wife
Declared the 1986 Act unconstitutional
Held that a divorced Muslim woman gets maintenance only for three months
Abolished all maintenance for Muslim women
explanation: Danial Latifi Constitution Bench harmonised the 1986 Act with Art 14/21: provision and maintenance must be made within iddat period, but to last for the wife's entire life or until remarriage.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; provision made within iddat must extend for entire life until remarriage.

learningObjective: Master Danial Latifi constitutional reconciliation.

question: Is there any upper monetary ceiling on maintenance under Section 144 BNSS (Section 125 CrPC)?
options: No, there is no statutory ceiling; the Magistrate may award such monthly allowance as he thinks fit
Yes, maximum Rs 5,000 per month
Yes, maximum Rs 10,000 per month
Yes, maximum Rs 1,500 per month
explanation: The CrPC Amendment Act, 2001 removed the archaic Rs 500 ceiling; both CrPC S. 125 and BNSS S. 144 prescribe no monetary ceiling (Magistrate awards reasonable amount).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; no statutory upper ceiling exists.
optionBreakdown.B: Rs 5,000 ceiling was in older state amendments (e.g., pre-2001 UP).
optionBreakdown.D: Old ceiling was Rs 500, omitted in 2001.

learningObjective: Recognize abolition of monetary ceiling in maintenance.

question: Under the Second Proviso to Section 144(1) BNSS (Section 125(1) CrPC), an application for interim maintenance and expenses of proceeding shall be disposed of:
options: Within sixty days from the date of the service of notice of the application to such person
Within thirty days
Within ninety days
Within six months
explanation: The Second Proviso to S. 144(1) BNSS / S. 125(1) CrPC mandates disposal of interim maintenance application within sixty days from notice.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; within sixty days from date of service of notice.

provision: BNSS S. 144(1) Proviso / CrPC S. 125(1) Proviso
learningObjective: Recall 60-day disposal timeline for interim maintenance.

question: In Rajnesh v. Neha ((2021) 2 SCC 324), what comprehensive directions were issued by the Supreme Court regarding maintenance proceedings?
options: Mandatory filing of an Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities by both parties, payment of maintenance from date of application, and overlapping maintenance adjustments across forums
Maintenance cannot be claimed in multiple forums under any circumstances
Interim maintenance must be paid in cash only
Wife must prove husband's income beyond reasonable doubt
explanation: Rajnesh v. Neha laid down pan-India guidelines: mandatory disclosure affidavits of assets and liabilities, uniform date of grant (from date of application), and adjustment across S. 125, HMA, and DV Act.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Rajnesh v. Neha comprehensive guidelines on disclosure affidavits and adjustment.
optionBreakdown.D: Standard is preponderance of probability, not reasonable doubt.

learningObjective: Master Rajnesh v. Neha maintenance framework.

question: Can a married daughter be compelled to maintain her aged father or mother under Section 144 BNSS (Section 125 CrPC)?
options: Yes, married daughters having independent means are equally liable to maintain parents unable to maintain themselves (Dr. Mrs. Vijaya Manohar Arbat v. Kashirao Rajaram Sawai)
No, only sons are liable under Section 125
Only unmarried daughters are liable
Parents can only claim from ancestral property
explanation: Vijaya Manohar Arbat ((1987) 2 SCC 278) settled that daughter (whether married or unmarried) who has independent means is liable to maintain her parents under S. 125 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; married daughter having independent means is liable.
optionBreakdown.C: Marriage does not destroy filial obligation.

learningObjective: Master daughter's liability to maintain parents.

question: Under Section 145 BNSS (Section 126 CrPC), proceedings for maintenance may be taken against any person in any district where:
options: He is, or where he or his wife resides, or where he last resided with his wife, or with the mother of the illegitimate child
Only where the husband's ancestral home is situated
Only where the marriage took place
Only in the High Court of the State
explanation: Section 145(1) BNSS / S. 126(1) CrPC provides flexible venue: where he is, where he or wife resides, or where he last resided with wife.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; wide venue options under Section 126 CrPC / Section 145 BNSS.
optionBreakdown.C: Place of marriage is not the primary venue clause in S. 126.

learningObjective: Recall territorial jurisdiction for maintenance proceedings.

question: Under the Proviso to Section 145(2) BNSS (Section 126(2) CrPC), within what time may an ex parte order of maintenance be set aside on good cause shown?
options: Within three months from the date of the order
Within thirty days
Within one year
Within six months
explanation: Section 145(2) Proviso BNSS / S. 126(2) Proviso CrPC specifies an application to set aside an ex parte order must be made within three months from date of order.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; within three months from date of order.

provision: BNSS S. 145(2) Proviso / CrPC S. 126(2) Proviso
learningObjective: Recall 3-month limitation to set aside ex parte maintenance order.

question: Under Section 144(3) BNSS (Section 125(3) CrPC), what is the limitation period for making an application to enforce arrears of maintenance?
options: Within a period of one year from the date on which the amount became due
Within three years
Within thirty days
Within twelve years
explanation: First Proviso to S. 144(3) BNSS / S. 125(3) CrPC bars warrant for recovery of any amount due unless application is made within one year from date due.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; within one year from date due.
optionBreakdown.B: Too long; S. 125 has a strict 1-year bar.
optionBreakdown.D: Article 136 of Limitation Act does not override S. 125(3) proviso.

provision: BNSS S. 144(3) Proviso / CrPC S. 125(3) Proviso
learningObjective: Master one-year limitation for recovery of maintenance arrears.

question: Under Section 144(3) BNSS (Section 125(3) CrPC), for breach of the order, what is the maximum imprisonment that a Magistrate may sentence the defaulter for each month's unpaid allowance?
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month or until payment if sooner made
Imprisonment up to 1 year
Imprisonment up to 3 years
Life imprisonment
explanation: Section 144(3) BNSS / S. 125(3) CrPC provides imprisonment up to one month for each month's unpaid allowance or until payment sooner made (Shahzada Khatoon v. Amjad Ali).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; up to one month for each month's default.

learningObjective: Master enforcement imprisonment limits for maintenance default.

question: Under Section 146 BNSS (Section 127 CrPC), when may a Magistrate alter or cancel a monthly allowance?
options: On proof of a change in the circumstances of the person receiving or paying the allowance, or upon relevant civil court decree
Only on the birthday of the child
Only if the State Government issues a notification
A maintenance order can never be altered
explanation: Section 146 BNSS (Section 127 CrPC) provides for alteration of allowance on proof of change in circumstances (income increase/decrease, price escalation, remarriage).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; on proof of change in circumstances or civil court decree.

learningObjective: Recall grounds for alteration of maintenance under S. 127 CrPC.

question: Under Section 146(3) BNSS (Section 127(3) CrPC), the Magistrate shall cancel an order of maintenance in favor of a divorced woman if:
options: She has remarried after the date of her divorce, or she has received the whole sum payable under customary/personal law upon divorce
She purchases a small car
She joins a part-time job earning Rs 1,000
The husband threatens her
explanation: Section 146(3) BNSS / S. 127(3) CrPC mandates cancellation where divorced woman has remarried or received customary sum on divorce.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; remarriage or receipt of customary lump-sum upon divorce.
optionBreakdown.C: Part-time job may affect quantum, not automatic cancellation.

learningObjective: Recall cancellation of maintenance on remarriage.

question: Under Section 147 BNSS (Section 128 CrPC), where may an order of maintenance be enforced?
options: In any place where the person against whom it is made may be, on the Magistrate being satisfied as to identity and non-payment
Only in the court which passed the original order
Only in the district where the marriage was registered
Only in the High Court
explanation: Section 147 BNSS (Section 128 CrPC) provides that an order of maintenance may be enforced by any Magistrate in any place where the defaulter may be.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; in any place where the defaulter may be.
optionBreakdown.B: Not limited to original issuing court.

learningObjective: Master pan-India enforcement of maintenance orders under S. 128 CrPC.

question: Does undergoing imprisonment under Section 125(3) CrPC / Section 144(3) BNSS wipe out or satisfy the liability to pay arrears of maintenance?
options: No; imprisonment is a mode of enforcement (coercive measure) and not a satisfaction of the debt; the liability to pay arrears remains alive
Yes, imprisonment wipes out all past arrears completely
Wipes out 50% of the arrears
The arrears become payable by the State Government
explanation: Kuldip Kaur v. Surinder Singh ((1989) 1 SCC 405) settled that imprisonment under S. 125(3) is coercive to compel payment; it does not wipe out or discharge the debt.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; imprisonment does not wipe out the liability for arrears.
optionBreakdown.B: Rejected; debtor cannot choose jail to avoid paying.

learningObjective: Master Kuldip Kaur ruling: imprisonment does not wipe out arrears.

question: How are maintenance arrears recovered under Section 144(3) BNSS (Section 125(3) CrPC)?
options: In the manner provided for levying fines (by issue of warrant for levy by attachment and sale of movable/immovable property under S. 421 CrPC / S. 461 BNSS)
By winding up the husband's employer company
By auctioning the husband's passport
Through international interpol notice
explanation: Section 144(3) BNSS / S. 125(3) CrPC directs that warrant for levying amount shall issue in the manner provided for levying fines.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; levied in the manner provided for levying fines.

learningObjective: Recall method of recovering maintenance arrears.

question: Under Section 145(2) BNSS (Section 126(2) CrPC), all evidence in maintenance proceedings shall be taken in the presence of:
options: The person against whom an order is proposed to be made, or when his personal attendance is dispensed with, in presence of his advocate
The District Magistrate
A public prosecutor only
A medical board
explanation: Section 145(2) BNSS / S. 126(2) CrPC requires evidence to be taken in presence of the respondent or his advocate, and recorded in manner prescribed for summons cases.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; taken in presence of person or his advocate.
optionBreakdown.C: Public prosecutor is not a party in S. 125.

learningObjective: Recall evidentiary procedure in maintenance inquiries.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 154 CrPC (Information in cognizable cases / FIR)?
options: Section 173 BNSS
Section 154 BNSS
Section 187 BNSS
Section 190 BNSS
explanation: Section 173 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 154 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 173 BNSS corresponds to Section 154 CrPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Section 154 BNSS is police arrest power.

learningObjective: Map Section 154 CrPC to Section 173 BNSS.

question: What revolutionary reform does Section 173(1) BNSS introduce regarding the registration of an FIR irrespective of the place where the crime was committed?
options: Statutorily codifies 'Zero FIR', mandating that information shall be registered irrespective of territorial jurisdiction and transferred to the police station having jurisdiction
Bans Zero FIR completely
Imposes a penalty of Rs 10,000 on complainant for filing outside jurisdiction
Allows police to discard out-of-jurisdiction complaints
explanation: Section 173(1) BNSS formally enacts 'Zero FIR': police MUST register information 'irrespective of the area where the offence was committed' and transfer to the jurisdictional police station.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory codification of Zero FIR in Section 173(1) BNSS.

learningObjective: Master statutory codification of Zero FIR in BNSS S. 173(1).

question: How has 'e-FIR' (electronic communication) been codified in Section 173(1) BNSS?
options: Information given electronically shall be taken on record, but must be signed by the person within three days before the FIR is formally registered
Information given electronically is automatically registered without any signature
Electronic information cannot be given by ordinary citizens
e-FIR is valid only for cyber offences
explanation: Section 173(1) Proviso BNSS provides that information given by electronic communication shall be taken on record, and on being signed within three days, it shall be registered as FIR.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; e-FIR taken on record and signed within 3 days.

learningObjective: Master 3-day signature requirement for e-FIR under BNSS.

question: In the Constitution Bench decision of Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P. ((2014) 2 SCC 1), what did the Supreme Court mandate regarding registration of FIR?
options: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence, and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such cases
Police have complete discretion to register or refuse FIR
Preliminary inquiry is mandatory in all cases before FIR
FIR can only be registered after obtaining Magistrate's permission
explanation: Lalita Kumari held that registration of FIR under S. 154 is mandatory where a cognizable offence is disclosed; preliminary inquiry is permitted only in 5 exceptions (medical negligence, corruption, matrimonial, commercial, delay).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory registration of FIR upon disclosure of cognizable offence.
optionBreakdown.C: Preliminary inquiry is the exception, not the rule.

learningObjective: Master Lalita Kumari mandatory FIR doctrine.

question: What new preliminary inquiry provision is codified in Section 173(3) BNSS for offences punishable between 3 to 7 years?
options: Police officer may, with prior permission of an officer not below DSP rank, proceed to conduct preliminary inquiry within 14 days to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists
Preliminary inquiry can last for 6 months
Police can dismiss the case without inquiry
Preliminary inquiry is conducted by the High Court
explanation: Section 173(3) BNSS incorporates a 14-day preliminary inquiry window for offences punishable between 3 and 7 years with DSP permission before FIR.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; preliminary inquiry within 14 days with DSP permission.

learningObjective: Master 14-day preliminary inquiry reform in BNSS S. 173(3).

question: Under Section 173(2) BNSS (Section 154(2) CrPC), a copy of the FIR shall be given to the informant:
options: Forthwith, free of cost
Within thirty days on payment of Rs 500
Only upon applying under the RTI Act
Only after filing of the charge-sheet
explanation: Section 173(2) BNSS (Section 154(2) CrPC) mandates that a copy of the information recorded shall be given forthwith, free of cost, to the informant.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; forthwith, free of cost.

learningObjective: Recall right to free copy of FIR.

question: Under Section 173(4) BNSS (Section 154(3) CrPC), if a station house officer refuses to record an FIR, to whom can the aggrieved person send the information by post?
options: To the Superintendent of Police concerned in writing
To the Chief Justice of India
To the Governor of the State
To the local municipal councillor
explanation: Section 173(4) BNSS (Section 154(3) CrPC) allows the aggrieved person to send substance of information to the Superintendent of Police, who may investigate or direct investigation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; send to Superintendent of Police.
optionBreakdown.B: CJI does not receive FIR complaints.

learningObjective: Recall remedy to SP upon refusal of FIR.

question: In Youth Bar Association of India v. Union of India ((2016) 9 SCC 473), what did the Supreme Court direct regarding uploading of FIRs online?
options: Copies of FIRs must be uploaded on the police website within 24 hours (or up to 48/72 hours in difficult areas) of registration, except sensitive cases like rape and terrorism
FIRs are top-secret documents that can never be uploaded online
Only the accused's consent can permit uploading
Uploading is prohibited under IT Act
explanation: Youth Bar Association mandated uploading FIRs within 24-48 hours on government/police websites to prevent arbitrary detentions and protect transparency.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; uploading on portal within 24-48 hours with sensitive offence exceptions.

learningObjective: Master Youth Bar Association online FIR mandate.

question: Can an FIR be registered on the basis of a cryptic telephone message received at the police station?
options: No; a cryptic, vague or anonymous telephone call does not constitute an FIR; it is only information for police to reach the spot (Tapinder Singh v. State of Punjab)
Yes, any telephonic ring is automatically an FIR
Yes, even a prank call must be an FIR
Only if recorded by an audio recorder
explanation: Tapinder Singh and Damodar v. State of Rajasthan settled that a cryptic message to rush to a spot without disclosing commission of a cognizable offence is not an FIR.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; cryptic telephone message is not an FIR.
optionBreakdown.D: Recording does not cure cryptic vagueness.

learningObjective: Analyze cryptic telephonic messages and FIR.

question: What is the evidentiary value of an FIR registered under Section 154 CrPC / Section 173 BNSS?
options: It is not substantive evidence; it can only be used under Sections 145 and 157 of Evidence Act to corroborate or contradict its maker (the informant)
It is conclusive proof of the facts stated therein
It binds the trial judge to convict the accused
It can be used to contradict any defence witness who did not write it
explanation: Aghnoo Nagesia and Hasib v. State of Bihar established that an FIR is not substantive evidence and can only corroborate or contradict the informant who lodged it.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; not substantive evidence; used only to corroborate or contradict maker.
optionBreakdown.B: Not substantive evidence or conclusive proof.

provision: BNSS S. 173 / BSA S. 148 & 160 / Aghnoo Nagesia
learningObjective: Master evidentiary value of FIR.

question: Under Section 175 BNSS (Section 156 CrPC), what is the power of a police officer to investigate cognizable cases?
options: May, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case which a Court having jurisdiction over the local area would have power to inquire into or try
Can only investigate after obtaining a warrant from High Court
Can only investigate if complainant pays fee
Cannot investigate without SP approval
explanation: Section 175(1) BNSS / S. 156(1) CrPC empowers police to investigate any cognizable case without an order of a Magistrate.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; investigate without Magistrate order in cognizable case.
optionBreakdown.B: No warrant needed for cognizable case.

learningObjective: Recall police power to investigate cognizable offences.

question: Under Section 175(3) BNSS (Section 156(3) CrPC), any Magistrate empowered under Section 190 CrPC / S. 210 BNSS may order:
options: Such an investigation as mentioned in subsection (1) by the police
Immediate execution of the accused
Dismissal of the High Court
Automatic conviction without trial
explanation: Section 175(3) BNSS (Section 156(3) CrPC) empowers the Magistrate to direct the police to register FIR and conduct investigation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Magistrate may order police investigation under S. 156(3).

learningObjective: Recall Magistrate power to order investigation under S. 156(3) CrPC.

question: Under Section 179 BNSS (Section 160 CrPC), who CANNOT be required to attend at any place other than their residence for police questioning?
options: Male under 15 years, male above 60 years, female, mentally or physically disabled person, or person with acute illness
Any person having a government job
Any advocate
Any business owner earning above Rs 10 lakhs
explanation: Section 179 BNSS (Section 160 CrPC) provides that male under 15, male over 60 (BNSS reduced from 65 to 60), woman, or disabled/ill person must be examined at residence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; protected vulnerable categories must be examined at residence.

learningObjective: Master protected categories examined at residence under S. 160 CrPC / S. 179 BNSS.

question: Under Section 180(2) BNSS (Section 161(2) CrPC), a witness examined by police is bound to answer truly all questions, EXCEPT:
options: Questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture
Questions regarding his name and address
Questions regarding what he saw with his own eyes
Questions asked after 5 PM
explanation: Section 180(2) BNSS / S. 161(2) CrPC codifies the constitutional right against self-incrimination (Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; exception for questions tending to incriminate the witness.

provision: BNSS S. 180(2) / CrPC S. 161(2) / Nandini Satpathy
learningObjective: Master right against self-incrimination during police examination.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani ((1978) 2 SCC 424) regarding Section 161(2) CrPC?
options: The protection against self-incrimination under Section 161(2) CrPC and Article 20(3) extends to suspects and witnesses alike during police interrogation
The protection applies only to a person formally facing a court trial
Police can use third-degree methods if the suspect refuses to answer
Section 161(2) is unconstitutional
explanation: Nandini Satpathy established that Article 20(3) and S. 161(2) protect any person from police coercion to extract self-incriminatory statements.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; protection extends to suspects and witnesses during interrogation.

learningObjective: Master Nandini Satpathy self-incrimination doctrine.

question: Under Section 181 BNSS (Section 162 CrPC), can a statement made by any person to a police officer in the course of an investigation be signed by the person making it?
options: No statement made by any person to a police officer in course of investigation shall, if reduced to writing, be signed by the person making it
Yes, signature is mandatory on all police statements
Signed only if the witness is an illiterate person
Signed only in murder cases
explanation: Section 181(1) BNSS / S. 162(1) CrPC expressly bars signing police statements: 'No statement made by any person to a police officer... shall be signed by the person making it.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory bar on signing statements made to police.

learningObjective: Recall bar on signing police investigation statements.

question: What modern technological method does the Proviso to Section 180(3) BNSS introduce for recording statements of witnesses under Section 161 CrPC?
options: Statement of witnesses may also be recorded by audio-video electronic means
Statements must be recorded on stone tablets
Statements can only be handwritten in fountain pen
Electronic recording is strictly barred
explanation: Section 180(3) Proviso BNSS allows recording statements of witnesses by audio-video electronic means, enhancing authenticity.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; audio-video electronic recording authorized.

learningObjective: Master audio-video recording of S. 161 statements under BNSS.

question: Under Section 181 BNSS (Section 162 CrPC), for what purpose may a statement recorded under Section 161 CrPC be used at trial?
options: Only by the accused, and with the permission of the court by the prosecution, to contradict such witness under Section 145 of Evidence Act (S. 148 BSA)
As substantive proof of the guilt of the accused
To corroborate the witness in chief examination
As a confession to convict the maker
explanation: Section 162 CrPC / Section 181 BNSS permits use of S. 161 statement ONLY to contradict the witness under S. 145 Evidence Act; it cannot be used for corroboration or substantive proof.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; strictly to contradict witness under S. 145 Evidence Act.

provision: BNSS S. 181 / CrPC S. 162 / BSA S. 148
learningObjective: Master limited use of S. 161 statements (contradiction only).

question: Under Section 182 BNSS (Section 163 CrPC), what is the statutory prohibition on police officers or persons in authority?
options: No police officer or person in authority shall offer or make any inducement, threat or promise as is mentioned in Section 24 of Evidence Act (S. 22 BSA)
Police may threaten witnesses to extract truth
Police can promise government jobs to confessing accused
Police can beat suspects in custody
explanation: Section 182 BNSS / S. 163 CrPC prohibits offering any inducement, threat or promise to extract statements.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory bar on inducement, threat, or promise.
optionBreakdown.D: Custodial violence is a serious crime.

learningObjective: Recall statutory bar on inducement/threat by police.

question: Under Section 176 BNSS (Section 157 CrPC), the police officer shall forthwith send a report of the cognizable offence (known as the 'Special Report') to:
options: A Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of such offence upon a police report
The High Court Registrar
The Chief Minister's office
The Union Home Minister
explanation: Section 176(1) BNSS / S. 157(1) CrPC requires police to forthwith send report to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance, to keep judicial check on investigation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; forthwith to Magistrate empowered to take cognizance.

learningObjective: Recall Special Report requirement to Magistrate under S. 157 CrPC.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 164 CrPC (recording of confessions and statements by Magistrate)?
options: Section 183 BNSS
Section 164 BNSS
Section 187 BNSS
Section 173 BNSS
explanation: Section 183 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 164 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 183 BNSS corresponds to Section 164 CrPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Section 164 BNSS is Section 145 CrPC (Land disputes).

learningObjective: Map Section 164 CrPC to Section 183 BNSS.

question: Under Section 183(2) BNSS (Section 164(2) CrPC), what warning MUST the Magistrate give to the accused before recording a confession?
options: That he is not bound to make a confession and that, if he does so, it may be used as evidence against him
That he will be pardoned if he confesses
That he will be beaten if he refuses to confess
That confession is compulsory under the penal code
explanation: Section 183(2) BNSS / S. 164(2) CrPC mandates warning: not bound to confess, and confession may be used as evidence against him; Magistrate must satisfy voluntariness.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory warning that he is not bound and it may be used against him.
optionBreakdown.B: Pardon is under S. 306 CrPC / S. 343 BNSS by tender, not S. 164 warning.

learningObjective: Master statutory warning required before recording confession.

question: Under Section 183(3) BNSS (Section 164(3) CrPC), if at any time before the confession is recorded, the person states that he is not willing to make the confession:
options: The Magistrate shall not authorise the detention of such person in police custody
The Magistrate shall order police to interrogate him further
The Magistrate can sentence him to 6 months for contempt
The Magistrate can record the confession anyway
explanation: Section 183(3) BNSS / S. 164(3) CrPC provides absolute protection: if person is unwilling, he CANNOT be remanded back to police custody (sent to judicial custody).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; shall not authorise detention in police custody.
optionBreakdown.B: Sending back to police custody is strictly prohibited.
optionBreakdown.C: Unwillingness is a right, not contempt.

learningObjective: Master bar on remanding unwilling confessor to police custody.

question: Under Section 183(1) BNSS, who can record a confession or statement under this section?
options: Any Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate, whether or not he has jurisdiction in the case
Only the Magistrate who will try the case
Only a police officer above SP rank
An Executive Magistrate in all cases
explanation: Section 183(1) BNSS / S. 164(1) CrPC empowers any Judicial Magistrate (whether having jurisdiction or not) to record confession or statement during investigation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; any Judicial Magistrate, whether having jurisdiction in the case or not.

learningObjective: Recall jurisdiction of Magistrates recording S. 164 statements.

question: Under Section 183(6) BNSS (Section 164(5A) CrPC), in offences of rape and sexual offences (Sections 64-71 BNS / 376 IPC), the statement of the victim shall be recorded:
options: By a woman Judicial Magistrate, or in her absence by a male Magistrate in presence of a woman, as soon as the commission of the offence is brought to notice
Only after the accused is arrested
In open court with public present
Only upon payment of court fee
explanation: Section 183(6) BNSS / S. 164(5A) CrPC mandates recording victim's statement by a woman Magistrate as soon as possible, in camera.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; by woman Magistrate as soon as offence brought to notice.
optionBreakdown.B: Arrest of accused not a prerequisite.

learningObjective: Master mandatory recording of sexual offence victim's statement by woman Magistrate.

question: What new technology requirement does Section 183(1) Proviso BNSS introduce for recording confessions and statements under Section 164 CrPC?
options: May also be recorded by audio-video electronic means in the presence of the advocate of the person accused
Recorded on magnetic cassette tapes only
Broadcast live on local court portal
No electronic recording is permitted
explanation: Section 183(1) Proviso BNSS explicitly provides that confessions and statements may be recorded by audio-video electronic means in presence of the accused's advocate.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; audio-video electronic means in presence of advocate.

learningObjective: Master audio-video recording of S. 164 statements under BNSS.

question: In Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1957 SC 637), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding 'cooling time' before recording a confession under Section 164 CrPC?
options: The accused should be given reasonable time (ordinarily at least 24 hours) to reflect in judicial custody away from police influence before confession is recorded
No cooling time is needed; record immediately while accused is frightened
Cooling time must be exactly one year
Cooling time can be spent in police lockup
explanation: Sarwan Singh established that reasonable cooling time (ordinarily 24 hours in judicial custody) is essential to eliminate police pressure before recording confession.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; reasonable cooling time (at least 24 hours) in judicial custody.
optionBreakdown.D: Must be away from police custody.

learningObjective: Master Sarwan Singh cooling time doctrine.

question: Can a confession recorded under Section 164 CrPC (Section 183 BNSS) be used as substantive evidence against the confessor?
options: Yes, a voluntary and truthful confession recorded by a Magistrate is substantive evidence and can form the sole basis of conviction if genuine
No, it can only be used to contradict him
No, it is inadmissible under Indian law
Only if corroborated by 10 eye-witnesses
explanation: Unlike a statement under S. 161, a confession properly recorded under S. 164 CrPC is substantive evidence and can support conviction if proven voluntary and true.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; substantive evidence capable of sustaining conviction if voluntary.
optionBreakdown.B: Confession is substantive, unlike S. 161 statements.
optionBreakdown.D: Corroboration is a rule of prudence, not mandatory 10 witnesses.

provision: BNSS S. 183 / BSA S. 22 / Shankaria v. State of Rajasthan
learningObjective: Master substantive evidentiary value of S. 164 confession.

question: What is the statutory memorandum that a Magistrate must append at the foot of a confession under Section 183(4) BNSS (Section 164(4) CrPC)?
options: A certificate stating: 'I have explained to [name] that he is not bound to make a confession... I believe that this confession was voluntarily made...'
A recommendation for 5 years sentence
A signature of the police investigating officer
A court stamp only without any text
explanation: Section 183(4) BNSS (Section 164(4) CrPC) mandates appending a specific statutory certificate signed by the Magistrate affirming voluntariness.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory memorandum certifying explanation and voluntary character.
optionBreakdown.B: Magistrate recording confession does not pass sentence.
optionBreakdown.C: Police must not be present or sign.

learningObjective: Recall statutory memorandum under S. 164(4) CrPC.

question: In Shivappa v. State of Karnataka ((1995) 2 SCC 76), what was held regarding the presence of police during recording of a confession under Section 164 CrPC?
options: The investigating officer and all police personnel must be completely excluded from the court room; presence of police vitiates the voluntary character of confession
Police must stand next to the accused with weapons drawn
Investigating officer must dictate the confession to the Magistrate
Police presence has no bearing on voluntariness
explanation: Shivappa established that exclusion of police from the room and sight of the accused is an indispensable safeguard to ensure voluntariness under S. 164 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; police must be completely excluded; presence vitiates voluntariness.

learningObjective: Master exclusion of police during S. 164 confession recording.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 167 CrPC (procedure when investigation cannot be completed in 24 hours)?
options: Section 187 BNSS
Section 167 BNSS
Section 173 BNSS
Section 190 BNSS
explanation: Section 187 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 167 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 187 BNSS corresponds to Section 167 CrPC.

learningObjective: Map Section 167 CrPC to Section 187 BNSS.

question: What is the historic structural change made in Section 187(2) BNSS regarding the timing of Police Custody compared to Section 167(2) CrPC?
options: Under Section 187(2) BNSS, the 15 days of police custody can be sought in whole or in parts at any time during the initial 40 or 60 days of the total detention period; under CrPC it had to be within the first 15 days only (CBI v. Anupam Kulkarni)
Police custody can now be granted for 365 days continuously
Police custody is abolished entirely in BNSS
Police custody can only be granted by the High Court
explanation: Under CrPC S. 167 as interpreted in Anupam Kulkarni (1992), police custody was permissible ONLY during the first 15 days. Section 187(2) BNSS allows 15 days police custody in parts across the initial 40 or 60 days.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; 15 days police custody can be spread across initial 40/60 days under BNSS S. 187(2).

provision: BNSS S. 187(2) / CrPC S. 167(2) / Anupam Kulkarni
learningObjective: Master revolutionary police custody spread reform in BNSS S. 187(2).

question: What are the outer limits of total detention (default bail periods) under Section 187(3) BNSS (Section 167(2) CrPC)?
options: 90 days where investigation relates to an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for not less than 10 years; and 60 days for any other offence
60 days for all offences universally
180 days for all cognizable offences
30 days for murder and 15 days for theft
explanation: Section 187(3) BNSS (Section 167(2) CrPC) provides 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10+ years; and 60 days for all other offences.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; 90 days for death/life/10+ years; 60 days for other offences.
optionBreakdown.C: 180 days applies under special statutes like UAPA/NDPS.

learningObjective: Recall 90/60 day default bail periods.

question: In Bikramjit Singh v. State of Punjab ((2020) 10 SCC 616) and M. Ravindran (2020), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding Default Bail under Section 167(2) CrPC?
options: Default bail is an indefeasible right and a fundamental right under Article 21; once the 60/90-day period expires and an application is filed, bail must be granted immediately regardless of subsequent filing of charge-sheet
Court can withhold default bail if the prosecutor requests 2 more days
Filing charge-sheet an hour later extinguishes the right to default bail
Default bail is a discretionary privilege
explanation: Bikramjit Singh established that default bail is an indefeasible fundamental right under Article 21 that crystallizes immediately upon expiry of the statutory period.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; indefeasible fundamental right under Art 21.
optionBreakdown.C: Subsequent charge-sheet cannot defeat already-availed right.

provision: BNSS S. 187 / CrPC S. 167(2) / Bikramjit Singh
learningObjective: Master indefeasible right to default bail.

question: Can an Executive Magistrate authorize detention under Section 187(4) BNSS (Section 167(2A) CrPC)?
options: Yes, when a Judicial Magistrate is not available, for a period not exceeding seven days in the aggregate
Yes, for up to 90 days
No, Executive Magistrates have no power of remand
Yes, for police custody of 30 days
explanation: Section 187(4) BNSS / S. 167(2A) CrPC empowers an Executive Magistrate to remand for a maximum period not exceeding seven days in aggregate when Judicial Magistrate is unavailable.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; up to seven days in aggregate when JM is unavailable.

learningObjective: Recall 7-day remand limit by Executive Magistrate.

question: Under Section 187(2) BNSS, how can production of the accused before the Magistrate be effected for remand?
options: In person or through the medium of electronic video linkage
Only in physical person without exception
Through a letter from the jailer
Through telephonic call
explanation: Section 187(2) BNSS codifies that production can be in person or through electronic video linkage for extending remand.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; in person or through video linkage.

learningObjective: Recall electronic video linkage production for remand.

question: In Rakesh Kumar Paul v. State of Assam ((2017) 15 SCC 67), how did the Supreme Court interpret 'not less than 10 years' in Section 167(2)(a)(i) CrPC?
options: 90 days applies ONLY where the minimum sentence is 10 years or more; where an offence carries imprisonment 'up to 10 years' (e.g., S. 386 IPC), the 60-day period applies
Up to 10 years always means 90 days
All IPC offences have 90 days
60 days applies only to bailable cases
explanation: Rakesh Kumar Paul established that 'not less than 10 years' means minimum 10 years; offences punishable 'up to 10 years' fall in the 60-day default bail bracket.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; 'up to 10 years' falls in 60-day bracket (Rakesh Kumar Paul).

learningObjective: Master Rakesh Kumar Paul 60 vs 90 day interpretation.

question: Under Section 187(2) BNSS, what must the Magistrate do if he authorizes detention in police custody?
options: Shall record his reasons in writing
Must inform the High Court within 1 hour
Must take signature of the complainant
Can grant police custody orally
explanation: Section 187(2) BNSS / S. 167(2) CrPC requires that no Magistrate shall authorize detention in police custody unless reasons are recorded in writing.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; must record reasons in writing.
optionBreakdown.B: Not required to inform HC in 1 hour.

learningObjective: Recall requirement to record reasons for police custody.

question: What is the consequence if the 90th or 60th day falls on a court holiday or Sunday, and the accused files a default bail application on the reopening day before the charge-sheet is filed?
options: The accused is entitled to default bail because limitation expired on the holiday and Section 10 of General Clauses Act does not extend detention (Achpal v. State of Rajasthan)
The police get an automatic extension because court was closed
The right to default bail is lost forever
Magistrate must reject the bail
explanation: Achpal and subsequent decisions hold that police cannot take benefit of court closure to extend period of detention beyond 60/90 days.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; court holiday does not extend detention period against accused.

learningObjective: Master court holiday and default bail computation.

question: Can an incomplete or defective charge-sheet filed without essential forensic/FSL reports prevent default bail?
options: No; an incomplete charge-sheet filed merely to defeat default bail does not extinguish the right under S. 167(2) CrPC / S. 187 BNSS
Yes, any paper labeled charge-sheet defeats default bail
Police can file a blank charge-sheet
Only if the High Court permits
explanation: A charge-sheet filed without completing substantive investigation (dummy charge-sheet) does not stop the default bail clock.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; incomplete dummy charge-sheet does not defeat default bail.

learningObjective: Analyze dummy charge-sheets and default bail.

question: Under Section 194 BNSS (Section 174 CrPC), an Inquest Report by police is prepared to ascertain:
options: The apparent cause of death, describing wounds, fractures and marks of injury, and in what manner or by what weapon they appear to have been inflicted
Who is guilty of murder and should be sentenced
The property dispute between heirs
The validity of the deceased's will
explanation: Podda Narayana v. State of A.P. (1975) established that the scope of inquest under S. 174 is limited strictly to ascertaining the apparent cause of death, not the murderer.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; apparent cause of death and physical injury marks.
optionBreakdown.B: Identifying murderer is for investigation, not inquest.

provision: BNSS S. 194 / CrPC S. 174 / Podda Narayana
learningObjective: Master limited scope of inquest under S. 174 CrPC / S. 194 BNSS.

question: Under Section 196 BNSS (Section 176 CrPC), in which cases is an Inquest by a Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate MANDATORY?
options: In any death, disappearance, or rape of a woman in custody of the police or in any other custody authorized by court
In all road traffic accidents
In natural deaths of elderly persons
Whenever requested by an MLA
explanation: Section 196(1A) BNSS / S. 176(1A) CrPC mandates inquiry by a Judicial Magistrate in cases of custodial death, custodial disappearance, or custodial rape.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory Judicial Magistrate inquiry for custodial death/rape.

learningObjective: Master mandatory Judicial Magistrate custodial inquest.

question: Which provision of BNSS 2023 corresponds to the Final Police Report (Charge-Sheet / Closure Report under Section 173 CrPC)?
options: Section 193 BNSS
Section 173 BNSS
Section 187 BNSS
Section 210 BNSS
explanation: Section 193 BNSS corresponds to Section 173 CrPC (report of police officer on completion of investigation / Charge-Sheet).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 193 BNSS corresponds to Section 173 CrPC.

learningObjective: Map Section 173 CrPC (Charge-Sheet) to Section 193 BNSS.

question: What statutory time limit does Section 193(1) BNSS prescribe for completing investigation in sexual offences against women and children?
options: Within two months from the date on which information was recorded by officer in charge of police station
Within six months
Within one year
Within twenty-four hours
explanation: Section 193(1) Proviso BNSS (Section 173(1A) CrPC) mandates that investigation in relation to rape/sexual offences shall be completed within two months.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; within two months from information date.

learningObjective: Recall 2-month investigation completion mandate for sexual offences.

question: What new duty does Section 193(3)(ii) BNSS impose on police regarding progress of investigation to the informant or victim?
options: Police officer shall inform the progress of investigation by all means including electronic communication to the informant or victim within ninety days
No information can ever be shared with informant
Police must inform the victim every 2 hours
Police must publish diary on social media
explanation: Section 193(3)(ii) BNSS is a significant victim-centric reform mandating progress communication within 90 days.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; progress update to informant/victim within 90 days.

learningObjective: Master 90-day progress reporting reform to victim under BNSS S. 193(3)(ii).

question: Under Section 193(9) BNSS (Section 173(8) CrPC), what power do the police have regarding Further Investigation?
options: Nothing precludes further investigation in respect of an offence after a report has been forwarded, and police may obtain further evidence and forward a supplementary report
Further investigation is completely banned once charge-sheet is filed
Police can conduct de novo re-investigation from scratch
Supplementary charge-sheet can only be filed by the CBI
explanation: Section 193(9) BNSS / S. 173(8) CrPC enables further investigation and supplementary report (Vinay Tyagi v. Irshad Ali). Note: re-investigation (de novo) is barred.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; further investigation and supplementary report permitted.
optionBreakdown.C: De novo re-investigation is barred for police without High Court order.

provision: BNSS S. 193(9) / CrPC S. 173(8) / Vinay Tyagi
learningObjective: Distinguish Further Investigation from Re-investigation.

question: In Bhagwant Singh v. Commissioner of Police ((1985) 2 SCC 537), what did the Supreme Court hold when police file a Closure Report (Final Report) under Section 173(2) CrPC?
options: Magistrate MUST issue notice to the informant/first informant and provide an opportunity of being heard before accepting the closure report
Magistrate can accept closure report silently without informing victim
Complainant has no locus standi once police conclude no offence
Closure report is final and cannot be challenged
explanation: Bhagwant Singh established the mandatory requirement of issuing notice to the first informant and hearing his Protest Petition before accepting a closure report.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; notice to informant and opportunity of being heard (Protest Petition).
optionBreakdown.D: Can be challenged by protest petition.

learningObjective: Master Bhagwant Singh notice rule on closure reports.

question: When a closure report is submitted by police under Section 173(2) CrPC, what options are open to the Magistrate?
options: (1) Accept closure report; (2) Disagree and take cognizance under S. 190(1)(b); (3) Order further investigation under S. 156(3); (4) Treat protest petition as a complaint under S. 200
Must accept the closure report blindly
Must transfer the case to High Court
Must dismiss the judicial service
explanation: Abhinandan Jha v. Dinesh Mishra (AIR 1968 SC 117) and Bhagwant Singh settled four distinct options available to the Magistrate upon receiving a closure report.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; four lawful options of Magistrate upon closure report.
optionBreakdown.B: Magistrate is not bound by police opinion.

learningObjective: Master four options of Magistrate on closure report.

question: Under Section 190 BNSS (Section 170 CrPC), if upon investigation it appears that there is sufficient evidence, the officer in charge of police station shall:
options: Forward the accused under custody to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance, or take security for his appearance if offence is bailable
Sentence the accused to 3 years
Release the accused unconditionally
Auction the accused's vehicle
explanation: Section 190 BNSS (Section 170 CrPC) provides for forwarding the accused to the Magistrate or taking bail if bailable.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; forward accused or take bail for appearance.

learningObjective: Recall forwarding accused under S. 170 CrPC / S. 190 BNSS.

question: Can a Magistrate compel the police to file a charge-sheet when the police have formed an opinion that no case is made out?
options: No; Magistrate cannot direct police to submit a charge-sheet, but Magistrate can take cognizance himself disagreeing with police (Abhinandan Jha v. Dinesh Mishra)
Yes, Magistrate can rewrite the police report directly
Yes, Magistrate can suspend the IO for filing closure
Police must follow Magistrate's order on who to charge
explanation: Abhinandan Jha established that formation of police opinion is within police domain; Magistrate cannot compel charge-sheet, but can disagree and take cognizance.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Magistrate cannot compel charge-sheet, but can take cognizance himself.

learningObjective: Master Abhinandan Jha police report independence doctrine.

question: What is the general ordinary place of inquiry and trial under Section 197 BNSS (Section 177 CrPC)?
options: Every offence shall ordinarily be inquired into and tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction it was committed
Court within whose jurisdiction the accused resides
Court within whose jurisdiction the victim resides
The Supreme Court of India
explanation: Section 197 BNSS (Section 177 CrPC) lays down the primary territorial rule: tried by court within whose local jurisdiction the offence was committed.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; court within whose local jurisdiction offence was committed.
optionBreakdown.B: Residence of accused is not general rule.
optionBreakdown.C: Residence of victim is exception in specific offences, not general rule.

learningObjective: Recall ordinary place of trial under S. 177 CrPC / S. 197 BNSS.

question: Under Section 198 BNSS (Section 178 CrPC), where an offence is committed partly in one local area and partly in another, it may be inquired into or tried by a court having jurisdiction over:
options: Any of such local areas
Only the local area where the offence started
Only the local area where the offence ended
Only the High Court of the State
explanation: Section 198 BNSS (Section 178 CrPC) provides that where an offence is committed partly in one and partly in another area, it may be tried by court in any of such areas.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; any of such local areas.

learningObjective: Recall multi-area jurisdiction rule.

question: Under Section 199 BNSS (Section 179 CrPC), when an act is an offence by reason of anything which has been done and of a consequence which has ensued, the offence may be tried by a court within whose local jurisdiction:
options: Any such thing has been done or any such consequence has ensued
Only where the act was done
Only where the consequence ensued
Only in Delhi
explanation: Section 199 BNSS (Section 179 CrPC) allows trial either where the act was done or where the consequence ensued.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; where act was done or consequence ensued.

learningObjective: Master act-and-consequence jurisdiction rule.

question: Under Section 201(4) BNSS (Section 181(4) CrPC), an offence of Criminal Misappropriation or Criminal Breach of Trust may be tried by a court within whose jurisdiction:
options: The offence was committed or any part of the property was received or retained, or was required to be returned or accounted for
Only where the contract was signed
Only where the bank branch is situated
Only in the capital of the State
explanation: Section 201(4) BNSS / S. 181(4) CrPC provides four alternative venues for CBT/misappropriation: where committed, received, retained, or required to be returned/accounted for.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; committed, received, retained, or required to be returned/accounted for.

learningObjective: Master four-fold jurisdiction in criminal breach of trust.

question: Under Section 201(1) BNSS (Section 181(1) CrPC), where may an offence of Thug or Dacoity (or dacoity with murder) be inquired into or tried?
options: By any court within whose local jurisdiction the offence was committed, or the accused person is found
Only where the dacoity was planned
Only in the State capital
Only in a Central Jail
explanation: Section 201(1) BNSS / S. 181(1) CrPC provides that dacoity, thug, or gang offence may be tried where committed or where accused is found.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; where offence committed or accused person is found.
optionBreakdown.B: Planning venue is additional, not exclusive.
optionBreakdown.D: Jail is not a court jurisdiction.

learningObjective: Recall jurisdiction in dacoity and thug offences.

question: Under Section 203 BNSS (Section 183 CrPC), an offence committed whilst the offender is in the course of performing a journey or voyage may be tried by a court:
options: Through or into the local jurisdiction of which the offender or the person against whom or thing in respect of which offence was committed, passed in course of journey
Only at the starting railway station
Only at the destination airport
Only by the Railway Protection Force
explanation: Section 203 BNSS (Section 183 CrPC) allows trial by any court along the transit route through which person or property passed during journey.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; any court along the route of the journey.

learningObjective: Recall jurisdiction for offences committed during journey.

question: Under Section 208 BNSS (Section 188 CrPC), when an offence is committed outside India by a citizen of India, or by a non-citizen on any ship/aircraft registered in India:
options: He may be dealt with in respect of such offence as if it had been committed at any place within India at which he may be found, provided previous sanction of Central Government is obtained
He cannot be tried in India under any circumstances
He can only be extradited to the foreign country
He can be tried without any Central Government sanction
explanation: Section 208 BNSS / S. 188 CrPC allows trial in India where person is found, but Proviso mandates previous sanction of Central Government.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; tried where found, subject to Central Government sanction.
optionBreakdown.C: India can try its own citizens.

learningObjective: Master extra-territorial jurisdiction and Central Government sanction under S. 188 CrPC.

question: In Thota Venkateswarlu v. State of A.P. ((2011) 9 SCC 527), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding the stage at which Central Government sanction under Section 188 CrPC is required?
options: Investigation can proceed and cognizance can be taken without prior sanction, but trial cannot commence without previous sanction of the Central Government
Sanction must be obtained before lodging FIR
Sanction is never needed if the victim is an Indian citizen
Sanction is needed only at the appellate stage
explanation: Thota Venkateswarlu held that sanction under S. 188 is not a condition precedent for FIR/investigation, but trial cannot commence without it.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; sanction is required before commencement of trial.

learningObjective: Master stage of S. 188 sanction.

question: Under Section 507 BNSS (Section 462 CrPC), what is the effect of a trial conducted in a wrong sessions division, district or local area?
options: No finding, sentence or order of any criminal court shall be set aside merely on ground of wrong local jurisdiction, unless it appears that such error has in fact occasioned a failure of justice
The entire trial is automatically void ab initio
The accused must be discharged immediately
The judge must be removed from service
explanation: Section 507 BNSS (Section 462 CrPC) is a curability provision: territorial irregularity does not vitiate trial unless actual failure of justice is proven.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; curable irregularity unless failure of justice is occasioned.
optionBreakdown.B: Territorial error does not render trial void per se.

learningObjective: Master curability of territorial error under S. 462 CrPC / S. 507 BNSS.

question: In Rupali Devi v. State of U.P. ((2019) 5 SCC 53), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding territorial jurisdiction for offences under Section 498A IPC?
options: Courts at the place where the wife takes shelter after leaving or being driven out of the matrimonial home have jurisdiction to try Section 498A offences, as cruelty creates adverse consequence at parental home
Only the court where the matrimonial home is situated has jurisdiction
Only the court where marriage took place has jurisdiction
Wife must file only in the High Court
explanation: Rupali Devi settled that mental cruelty continues at the shelter/parental home, giving courts at the wife's shelter home territorial jurisdiction under S. 179 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; court where wife takes shelter has jurisdiction under S. 179 CrPC.

learningObjective: Master Rupali Devi jurisdiction rule for matrimonial cruelty.

question: Under Section 210(1) BNSS (Section 190(1) CrPC), in how many ways may a Magistrate take cognizance of an offence?
options: Three ways: (a) upon receiving a complaint; (b) upon a police report; (c) upon information received from any person other than a police officer, or upon his own knowledge
Only upon a police charge-sheet
Only upon a complaint in writing by an advocate
Ten ways
explanation: Section 210(1) BNSS / S. 190(1) CrPC specifies exactly three modes of taking cognizance: (a) complaint; (b) police report; (c) suo motu / other information.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; three statutory modes of taking cognizance.
optionBreakdown.B: Police report is only one mode.

learningObjective: Recall three modes of taking cognizance.

question: What does 'taking cognizance' mean in criminal jurisprudence?
options: It means judicial application of mind to the suspected commission of an offence for the purpose of taking further procedural steps to proceed against the offender (R.R. Chari v. State of U.P.)
It means convicting and sentencing the accused
It means arresting the accused in open court
It means framing charges
explanation: R.R. Chari and Chief Enforcement Officer v. Videocon held that cognizance is taking judicial notice of an offence to initiate judicial proceedings.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; judicial application of mind to initiate criminal process.
optionBreakdown.C: Cognizance is on offence, not physical arrest.
optionBreakdown.D: Framing charge is a subsequent trial stage.

learningObjective: Define taking cognizance of offence.

question: Does a Magistrate take cognizance of the 'offender' or the 'offence'?
options: Cognizance is always taken of the OFFENCE, not the offender; once cognizance of an offence is taken, the court has duty to proceed against all perpetrators
Cognizance is taken exclusively of the person named in the FIR
Cognizance is taken only of government servants
Cognizance is taken of the defence counsel
explanation: Raghubans Dubey v. State of Bihar (AIR 1967 SC 1167) established that cognizance is taken of an offence, and court can summon anyone who appears involved under S. 190/319.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; cognizance is of the offence, not the offender.
optionBreakdown.B: Court is not restricted to persons named in police report.

learningObjective: Master principle: cognizance is of the offence, not the offender.

question: Under Section 211 BNSS (Section 191 CrPC), when a Magistrate takes cognizance under clause (c) (suo motu / other information):
options: The accused shall, before any evidence is taken, be informed that he is entitled to have the case inquired into or tried by another Magistrate
The accused must plead guilty immediately
The case must be transferred to the High Court
The Magistrate can try the case without giving any option
explanation: Section 211 BNSS (Section 191 CrPC) provides a vital safeguard against bias: accused must be informed of right to have case transferred to another Magistrate.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; accused must be informed of right to transfer case to another Magistrate.
optionBreakdown.C: Transferred to CJM or another JM, not HC.

learningObjective: Recall transfer safeguard when cognizance taken suo motu.

question: Under Section 213 BNSS (Section 193 CrPC), can a Court of Session take cognizance of any offence as a court of original jurisdiction?
options: No, except as otherwise expressly provided by law, a Court of Session shall not take cognizance of any offence as a court of original jurisdiction unless committed to it by a Magistrate
Yes, all murder cases must be filed directly in Court of Session
Yes, Sessions Court has concurrent original filing jurisdiction
Only if the High Court Chief Justice directs orally
explanation: Section 213 BNSS (Section 193 CrPC) creates a statutory bar: Court of Session cannot take cognizance of any offence as original court without committal, unless express exception applies (e.g. defamation of high dignitary).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Court of Session cannot take cognizance without committal.
optionBreakdown.B: Must be committed by Magistrate under S. 209 CrPC / S. 232 BNSS.
optionBreakdown.D: Statutory rule cannot be bypassed orally.

learningObjective: Master committal bar on Sessions Court original cognizance.

question: Under Section 218 BNSS (Section 197 CrPC), previous sanction of Central or State Government is mandatory before taking cognizance of an offence alleged to have been committed by:
options: Any Judge, Magistrate, or public servant not removable from office save by or with sanction of Government, while acting or purporting to act in discharge of official duty
Any private citizen
Any clerk in a private commercial bank
Any municipal sweeper
explanation: Section 218 BNSS (Section 197 CrPC) provides statutory protection against vexatious prosecution for judges, magistrates and senior public servants for acts in discharge of official duty.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; judges, magistrates, and senior public servants acting in official duty.
optionBreakdown.B: Private citizens have no sanction protection.
optionBreakdown.D: Only public servants removable by Government.

learningObjective: Master prosecution sanction under S. 197 CrPC / S. 218 BNSS.

question: In Matajog Dobey v. H.C. Bhari (AIR 1956 SC 44), what test was laid down for determining whether an act requires sanction under Section 197 CrPC?
options: There must be a reasonable connection between the act and the official duty; it must not be a fanciful claim, but lie within scope and range of official duties
Any crime committed by a public servant is automatically protected
Taking a bribe is an act in discharge of official duty
Sanction is never required if the police officer is in uniform
explanation: Matajog Dobey established the 'reasonable nexus' test: the act must have reasonable connection with official duty so that it can be reasonably claimed to have been done in official capacity.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; reasonable connection / nexus test between act and official duty.
optionBreakdown.C: Bribe taking has no nexus with official duty.
optionBreakdown.D: Uniform alone does not grant immunity.

learningObjective: Master Matajog Dobey reasonable nexus test for S. 197 sanction.

question: What new time limit does Section 218(1) Proviso BNSS introduce for the Government to decide on an application for sanction to prosecute a public servant?
options: The Government shall take a decision within a period of one hundred and twenty days (120 days), failing which sanction shall be deemed to have been accorded
Within thirty days
Within five years
No time limit exists
explanation: Section 218(1) Proviso BNSS introduces a revolutionary 120-day timeline for deciding sanction, incorporating deemed sanction to prevent indefinite government stonewalling.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; 120 days with deemed sanction reform in BNSS S. 218(1).

learningObjective: Master 120-day deemed sanction reform in BNSS S. 218.

question: Under Section 221 BNSS (Section 198 CrPC), who alone can file a complaint for prosecution of offences against marriage (Chapter V BNS / Chapter XX IPC)?
options: Some person aggrieved by the offence (ordinarily the husband or wife)
Any stranger on the street
Any police officer without victim's consent
The District Magistrate on suo motu complaint
explanation: Section 221 BNSS (Section 198 CrPC) mandates that no court shall take cognizance of matrimonial offences except upon complaint made by some person aggrieved.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; only person aggrieved (husband/wife or specified relatives).
optionBreakdown.C: Police cannot file without aggrieved person.

learningObjective: Recall person aggrieved requirement for matrimonial offences.

question: Under Section 222 BNSS (Section 199 CrPC), who can file a complaint for Defamation (Section 356 BNS / Section 500 IPC)?
options: No court shall take cognizance except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence
Any member of the public
Police can lodge an FIR on their own
The High Court Registrar suo motu
explanation: Section 222 BNSS / S. 199 CrPC provides that prosecution for defamation can only be initiated on a private complaint by the person aggrieved (defamed person).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; only upon complaint by person defamed/aggrieved.
optionBreakdown.C: Defamation is non-cognizable; police cannot file FIR.

learningObjective: Recall person aggrieved rule for defamation prosecution.

question: Which provision of BNSS 2023 corresponds to Section 200 CrPC (examination of complainant)?
options: Section 223 BNSS
Section 200 BNSS
Section 210 BNSS
Section 227 BNSS
explanation: Section 223 BNSS corresponds to Section 200 CrPC (examination of complainant and witnesses present on oath).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 223 BNSS corresponds to Section 200 CrPC.
optionBreakdown.D: Section 227 BNSS is dismissal of complaint.

learningObjective: Map Section 200 CrPC to Section 223 BNSS.

question: What new mandatory safeguard does the First Proviso to Section 223(1) BNSS introduce regarding complaints?
options: No cognizance of an offence shall be taken by the Magistrate without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard
Accused must be arrested before examination of complainant
Complainant must pay Rs 50,000 security
All complaints must be referred to mediation for 1 year
explanation: Section 223(1) Proviso BNSS introduces a groundbreaking protection for the accused: no cognizance on complaint shall be taken without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; opportunity of hearing to accused before cognizance on complaint.

learningObjective: Master pre-cognizance hearing to accused under BNSS S. 223(1).

question: Under Section 223(1) BNSS (Section 200 CrPC), how does a Magistrate examine the complainant and witnesses present?
options: Upon oath, and the substance of such examination shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed by the complainant and the witnesses, and also by the Magistrate
Orally without any oath
Through police interrogation
By tape recording only without signature
explanation: Section 223(1) BNSS / S. 200 CrPC requires examination on oath, substance reduced to writing, and signed by complainant, witnesses and Magistrate.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; on oath, reduced to writing, signed by complainant, witnesses and Magistrate.

learningObjective: Recall procedure for examining complainant under S. 200 CrPC.

question: Under Section 225 BNSS (Section 202 CrPC), when is an inquiry by Magistrate or investigation by police MANDATORY before issuing process?
options: Where the accused is residing at a place beyond the area in which the Magistrate exercises his jurisdiction
Whenever the accused is wealthy
Whenever the offence is punishable with fine only
Whenever the complainant is a woman
explanation: Section 225(1) BNSS / S. 202(1) CrPC mandates inquiry or investigation where the accused resides outside the territorial jurisdiction of the Magistrate (to curb false outstation harassment).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory where accused resides beyond local jurisdiction.
optionBreakdown.C: Applies across all offences where accused is outstation.

learningObjective: Master mandatory inquiry under S. 202 CrPC for outstation accused.

question: In National Bank of Oman v. Barakara Abdul Aziz ((2013) 2 SCC 488), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding non-compliance with the amended Section 202 CrPC?
options: Inquiry or investigation under Section 202 is mandatory where the accused resides beyond local jurisdiction, and issuance of process without it is completely illegal
Section 202 is merely discretionary and can be ignored
Magistrate can issue arrest warrant without any inquiry
Accused residing outside district cannot challenge process
explanation: National Bank of Oman held that post-2005 amendment, S. 202 inquiry is mandatory for outstation accused, and issuing summons without it vitiates the order.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory inquiry; issuance of process without it is illegal.

provision: BNSS S. 225 / National Bank of Oman (2013)
learningObjective: Master National Bank of Oman outstation inquiry rule.

question: Under Section 226 BNSS (Section 203 CrPC), when may a Magistrate dismiss a complaint?
options: If, after considering the statements on oath and result of inquiry/investigation under S. 202, there is in his judgment no sufficient ground for proceeding, recording reasons briefly
Whenever the complainant fails to bring an advocate
Whenever police advise dismissal orally
Only if the accused pleads not guilty
explanation: Section 226 BNSS (Section 203 CrPC) empowers the Magistrate to dismiss complaint if in his judgment there is no sufficient ground for proceeding, recording brief reasons.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; dismiss if no sufficient ground for proceeding, recording reasons.
optionBreakdown.D: Dismissal is before accused is summoned.

learningObjective: Recall grounds for dismissal of complaint under S. 203 CrPC.

question: Under Section 227 BNSS (Section 204 CrPC), what process shall the Magistrate issue if in his opinion there is sufficient ground for proceeding?
options: In a summons-case, a summons; in a warrant-case, he may issue a warrant, or, if he thinks fit, a summons for causing the accused to appear
A death warrant in all cases
A search warrant for the accused's bank account
An order of attachment of property
explanation: Section 227(1) BNSS / S. 204(1) CrPC specifies: in summons-case, summons; in warrant-case, summons or warrant (summons preferred initially).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; summons in summons-case; summons or warrant in warrant-case.
optionBreakdown.C: Issue of process is for personal appearance.

learningObjective: Recall process to be issued under S. 204 CrPC / S. 227 BNSS.

question: Under Section 227(2) BNSS (Section 204(2) CrPC), no summons or warrant shall be issued against the accused under subsection (1) until:
options: A list of the prosecution witnesses has been filed
The complainant pays Rs 10,000 cash
The accused admits the charges
The High Court grants permission
explanation: Section 227(2) BNSS / S. 204(2) CrPC provides: 'No summons or warrant shall be issued against the accused under sub-section (1) until a list of the prosecution witnesses has been filed.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; list of prosecution witnesses must be filed first.

learningObjective: Recall witness list prerequisite for issue of process.

question: In Pepsi Foods Ltd. v. Special Judicial Magistrate ((1998) 5 SCC 749), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding the summoning of an accused in a criminal case?
options: Summoning of an accused in a criminal case is a serious matter; criminal law cannot be set into motion as a matter of course; the Magistrate must carefully scrutinize allegations and evidence before issuing process
Magistrate must issue summons mechanically whenever a complaint is filed
Corporate directors must always be summoned without inquiry
Summoning order cannot be challenged under Section 482 CrPC
explanation: Pepsi Foods established that summoning an accused affects personal liberty and dignity; the Magistrate must apply judicial mind to prima facie evidence before issuing process.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; summoning is a serious matter requiring careful judicial scrutiny.

learningObjective: Master Pepsi Foods summoning scrutiny doctrine.

question: Under Section 228 BNSS (Section 205 CrPC), when may a Magistrate dispense with the personal attendance of the accused?
options: Whenever a Magistrate issues a summons, he may, if he sees reason so to do, dispense with the personal attendance of the accused and permit him to appear by his advocate
Only if the accused pays a fine of Rs 1 lakh
Only in civil cases
Personal attendance can never be dispensed with
explanation: Section 228(1) BNSS / S. 205(1) CrPC allows Magistrate issuing summons to dispense with personal attendance and permit appearance through advocate.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; dispense with personal attendance and permit appearance by advocate.

learningObjective: Recall dispensing with personal attendance under S. 205 CrPC / S. 228 BNSS.
